title: Post-Anesthesia Care Unit
summary: Receive a patient in the PACU, run a safe handover and react to a drowsy patient with airway obstruction.
scenario: A patient has just arrived in the post-anesthesia care unit after general anesthesia. You are the recovery nurse. Prioritise airway and breathing, receive a structured handover, detect unsafe care and respond to a deteriorating patient.
objectives: Identify the essential elements of a handover
Respond to airway obstruction in recovery

patient.procedure: Elective hernia repair, general anesthesia (about 90 minutes)

history: Extubated in the operating room, transferred with oxygen
Analgesia plan as ordered by the anesthesiologist (see anesthesia record)

steps.title: Arrival priorities
steps.prompt: Arrange your actions when the patient arrives in the PACU.

items.text: Check airway patency and breathing, and give supplemental oxygen as ordered
Attach standard monitors and record initial vital signs
Receive a structured handover from the anesthesia team
Assess pain, nausea, temperature and the surgical site
Document and reassess at regular intervals

steps.explanation: Airway and breathing come first. Monitors give objective data, then the handover fills in context. Symptoms are assessed next, and everything is documented and reassessed at regular intervals.
steps.takeaway: Airway and breathing first, then monitors, handover and full assessment.

steps.title: Handover content
steps.prompt: Which information is essential in the handover from the anesthesia team?

options.text: Identity, procedure, anesthetic technique, allergies, intra-operative events and the post-operative plan
Only the surgeon's name and the ward number
Only the drugs that were given

steps.explanation: A good handover gives the recovery nurse what is needed to care for the patient safely: who the patient is, what happened, what to watch for and what the plan is.
steps.takeaway: Handover = who, what happened, what to watch for, what next.

steps.title: Recovery care review
steps.instruction: Select every entry that shows unsafe care.
steps.situation: Fifteen minutes after arrival, you review the recovery record and the bedside.

items.label: Suction and bag-mask device available at the bedside
Pain score documented using a numeric scale
Temperature checked, warm blanket provided
items.why: Appropriate for a mildly low temperature.

items.label: Snoring respirations noted, no action taken because 'he is just sleeping'
items.why: Snoring is a sign of partial airway obstruction and needs action.

items.label: Patient left alone for 20 minutes while staff took a break
items.why: Patients in recovery need continuous observation by a trained person.

steps.explanation: Snoring indicates partial upper-airway obstruction, and a patient recovering from anesthesia must never be left unobserved.
steps.takeaway: Snoring is an airway sign, not a sign of good sleep.

steps.title: Drowsy and snoring
steps.situation: The patient is drowsy and making snoring sounds. SpO₂ has fallen to 90% and the respiratory rate is 8 per minute.

options.text: Open the airway (chin lift or jaw thrust), stimulate the patient, make sure oxygen is delivered and call the anesthesiologist
options.consequence: The airway is opened, oxygen delivery is confirmed and help is on its way.

options.text: Increase the oxygen and observe quietly for another 15 minutes
options.consequence: Oxygen helps, but the cause is airway obstruction. Without opening the airway and calling for help, the patient may worsen.

options.text: Leave him to sleep: snoring is normal after anesthesia
options.consequence: Snoring with falling SpO₂ and slow breathing is not normal. The airway is at risk.

options.text: Write the values in the record and continue paperwork
options.consequence: Documentation is important but cannot replace immediate action.

steps.explanation: Snoring with falling SpO₂ and a slow respiratory rate signals airway obstruction and inadequate ventilation. Open the airway, stimulate, confirm oxygen and get help.
steps.takeaway: Airway first: open it, give oxygen, call for help.

steps.title: Follow-up: no air movement
steps.situation: SpO₂ is 86%. The patient does not respond to your voice and you see chest effort but hear no air movement.

options.text: Call for urgent help and support airway and ventilation with a bag-mask and oxygen until the anesthesiologist arrives
Move the patient to the ward
Ask the family to wake him

steps.explanation: Chest effort without air movement means a complete airway obstruction. It is an emergency: call for help and support the airway and ventilation immediately.
steps.takeaway: Effort without air movement is an emergency. Call for help and support the airway.

steps.title: Recovery scoring
steps.prompt: Which parameters make up the modified Aldrete score, commonly used to judge readiness to leave the PACU?

options.text: Activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness and oxygen saturation
Heart rate, hemoglobin, glucose, sodium and potassium
Duration of surgery, type of surgery, surgeon and blood loss

steps.explanation: The modified Aldrete score covers five areas: activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness and oxygen saturation. Many units also use additional criteria such as pain and nausea.
steps.takeaway: Aldrete: activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness, SpO₂.

steps.title: Bedside readiness
steps.instruction: Select the items that should be ready at every PACU bedside.

items.label: Continuous ECG, SpO₂ and blood pressure monitoring
Emergency call system and access to a resuscitation trolley
Anesthesia gas vaporizer
items.why: Part of the anesthesia machine, not the recovery bed.

steps.explanation: The bedside needs oxygen, suction, ventilation and airway equipment, monitors and a way to call for help. Operating-room items do not belong there.
steps.takeaway: Every recovery bed is ready for an airway emergency.
